chapter: Ella, Charlie Christian and Europe with Hayes
title: William Woody Michener, the baritone player
summary: Michener, a well-educated, cheerful baritone saxophonist and Clarke's confidant on the European tour, died of tuberculosis in 1939.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: No. Well, there was one, William Woody Michener, he was our baritone player. He made the European tour with us.
And we called him Happy, you know, because he was always happy.
He always had a big smile on his face.
Always. Very seldom -- I had never seen him angry at all. So he was my buddy, you know?
And I would talk to him about things because he was very well educated. His father was one of the leading doctors in his home town, and he was from Cleveland or somewhere in the vicinity.
And his father was a wonderful doctor. And William had a wonderful education and I could talk to him and he seemed to understand everything, you know.
Because I imagine his father had raised him, you know, like he should be raised.
So I could talk. There was never any slang words, or you know, he was always correct.
So I always confided in William Woody.
Because he was older than you.
No, let's see, he was 25. Well, he died at 25 in 19 -- no he was 26, he was a year older than me. He was 26 in 193 -- he died in 1939 and he was 26. I was 25.

Tuberculosis. And his father -- well, he wanted to be a musician, so his father told him -- you know, how it is -- "Well, son, okay, you finish your studies and you -- now it's up to you. I'm not going to stop you, but take care of yourself." And he tried to stop him from smoking. He said, "Don't smoke cigarettes," and he'd smoke, smoke, smoke, smoke, you know. And then we went to Europe, I think the weather got to him too, because we were in Sweden in November, December and January, and February, you know, in Scandinavia.
And I think the weather got to him, because it got to me too, you know?
